meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Duty makes us do things well, but love makes us do them beautifully'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Zig Ziglar. The line was credited to Phillips Brooks in an 1916 teachers' journal — a decade before Ziglar was born.

answer.label: Not Zig Ziglar — attributed to Phillips Brooks
answer.sourceLine: This maxim was already in print crediting the Boston clergyman Phillips Brooks in the teachers’ journal Primary Education in 1916 — a decade before Zig Ziglar was born (1926) — so Ziglar cannot be its source. That said, the Brooks credit itself traces only to that posthumous periodical, not to any located sermon or letter in his own hand, so treat it as a long-standing attribution rather than a pinned primary source.

source.heading: Where the line actually shows up

docMeta.dd: Not located — no sermon or letter pinned

source.excerpt: Duty makes us do things well, but love makes us do them beautifully.
trail: Primary Education, a Boston teachers’ monthly, printed the line crediting Phillips Brooks on p. 190 of its 1916 volume — decades before Ziglar’s career.
Wikiquote lists it among Brooks’s sourced quotes, though the underlying citation is that 1916 journal, not a work by Brooks himself.
Modern quote sites such as this one and the official Zig Ziglar social accounts recirculate the line under Ziglar’s name with no source, which is how the misattribution spread.
source.excerptNote: The wording is stable across a century of reprints; what shifts is only the name attached to it — from Phillips Brooks in the 1910s to Zig Ziglar in the internet era.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented appearance of this exact wording is in Primary Education (1916), which predates the U.S. 1931 public-domain cutoff, and the man it credits — Phillips Brooks — died in 1893, so any work of his is long in the public domain. Because no specific Brooks text has been located, the safest anchor is the pre-1931 periodical appearance.

author.name: Phillips Brooks
author.kicker: The name behind the oldest credit
author.heading: Who was Phillips Brooks?
author.bio: Phillips Brooks was one of the most celebrated American preachers of the 19th century, long rector of Trinity Church in Boston and, briefly, Bishop of Massachusetts. He is best remembered today as the author of the Christmas carol O Little Town of Bethlehem (1868), and his sermons and aphorisms circulated widely in inspirational and educational literature well after his death in 1893.

misattribution.heading: How Zig Ziglar got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” case: an old, uplifting one-liner drifts onto a famous modern motivator who never claimed to have coined it.

items.why: Goodreads, Quotefancy, Pinterest and even the official Zig Ziglar Facebook page circulate the line as Ziglar’s, but it was in print crediting Brooks before Ziglar was even born, so he cannot be the originator.

The 1916 journal Primary Education (p. 190) credits Brooks, and Lib Quotes and Wikiquote follow it — but neither points to a sermon or letter Brooks actually wrote, so his authorship remains a long-standing attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: this is not a Zig Ziglar original. The oldest documented credit, back to 1916, names Phillips Brooks — though even that rests on a periodical, not on any work found in Brooks’s own hand.

context.heading: Why the mix-up is so tidy
lead: Phillips Brooks belonged to an era whose pulpit maxims flooded schoolroom readers, autograph albums and teachers’ magazines — exactly the kind of anonymous-feeling, uplifting sentiment that survives long after its context is forgotten. Zig Ziglar, a generation later, built a career reciting and popularizing such lines, and the internet did the rest, quietly swapping the old clergyman’s name for the famous motivator’s.

The honest verdict sits in the middle: the wording is genuine and old, the Ziglar credit is wrong, and the Brooks credit is the best we have — but it rests on a 1916 journal rather than on a page Brooks himself is known to have written.
context.pull: The line is old and real; only the name on it keeps changing.
